title: Stack
summary: Last in, first out. Add and remove only at the top — which is exactly the shape of anything that must be undone in reverse order.

analogy.beginner: A pile of plates. You put a clean plate on top and you take the top plate off. You never pull one from the middle — the pile would collapse. The last plate you put down is the first one you pick up.
analogy.interview: A LIFO collection with O(1) push, pop and peek. Backed by an array with a top index, or by a singly linked list with head insertion. In Java, use `ArrayDeque` — `java.util.Stack` extends `Vector` and is synchronised legacy.

intuition:
A stack is the data structure of *pending work* and *undo*.

Whenever you start something you cannot finish until you first finish something else, you have a stack. Reading a nested expression: you meet `(` and must remember it until the matching `)`. Calling a function: you must remember where to return before you can run the callee. Browsing: each page you leave waits for you to come back.

The defining property is that things come out in *reverse* order. If reverse order is what the problem needs, a stack is almost certainly the answer — and the restriction to one end is not a limitation, it is what makes every operation O(1).

problemFirst.motivatingProblem: Check whether a string of brackets is balanced: `{[()]}` is valid, `{[(])}` is not.

bruteForce.idea: Count the brackets — as many `(` as `)`. Or repeatedly delete adjacent matching pairs until nothing changes.
code: return open == 0;   // says ")(" is valid. It is not.
bruteForce.whySlow: Counting ignores order, so it accepts `)(`. Repeated deletion is correct but rebuilds the whole string on every pass — O(n) passes × O(n) work each.

problemFirst.observation: When we meet a closing bracket, the only bracket it may legally match is the *most recent* unmatched opening bracket. Nothing older matters.
problemFirst.leap: 'Most recent unmatched thing' is exactly what a stack gives you in O(1). Push every opener; on a closer, pop and check the pair. One pass, O(n).

howItWorks: **pop()** — remove and return the top. O(1). Throws or returns null if empty, so check `isEmpty()` first.
**peek()** — look at the top without removing it. O(1).
Array-backed: keep an index `top`; push writes `a[top++]`, pop reads `a[--top]`. Grows by doubling.
List-backed: insert and remove at the head; no resizing, but an object per element and worse cache behaviour.

signals: Matching or nesting: brackets, tags, nested structures
'Next greater / next smaller element' → monotonic stack
Converting a recursive solution to an iterative one
antiSignals: You need first-in-first-out order (that is a Queue)
You need access to the middle or to arbitrary positions

code: int top = stack.peek(); // look at the top
int out = stack.pop();  // remove the top

implementations.label: Simple
implementations.explanation: A stack built on a plain array, so you can see that push and pop are just an index moving up and down.
code: private int top = 0;              // next free slot
if (top == 0) throw new NoSuchElementException("stack is empty");
if (top == 0) throw new NoSuchElementException("stack is empty");

implementations.label: Optimized
implementations.explanation: In real code use `ArrayDeque`. It is faster and unsynchronised, unlike the legacy `java.util.Stack`. The balanced-brackets solution below is the canonical interview answer — note the two failure modes: a closer with an empty stack, and leftovers at the end.
code: case '(' -> stack.push(')');   // push what we EXPECT to see
return stack.isEmpty();   // leftovers mean unclosed brackets

complexity.time: push O(1) · pop O(1) · peek O(1) · search O(n)
complexity.why: All operations touch only one end, so no element ever has to move to make room — unlike inserting into the middle of an array. Array-backed push is O(1) amortised because doubling makes the occasional copy rare. Searching is O(n) because a stack deliberately gives you no way to look inside; if you need that, you have picked the wrong structure.

commonMistakes.fix: `)))` pops an empty stack. Check first — it is also the classic missed edge case in the brackets problem.

commonMistakes.mistake: Forgetting to check the stack is empty at the end
commonMistakes.fix: `(((` never fails during the loop but is still invalid. Leftovers mean unclosed openers.
It extends `Vector`, so every operation is synchronised and slower. Use `ArrayDeque`.
`push` adds at the head, `add` adds at the tail. Mixing them silently turns your stack into a queue.

realWorldUses: The JVM call stack — every method call pushes a frame; `StackOverflowError` is that stack overflowing.
Undo/redo in editors; the browser back button.
Expression evaluation and syntax parsing in compilers; JSON and XML parsers matching nesting.
Depth-first search, when written iteratively, is a stack replacing the recursion.
interviewNotes: The monotonic stack (keeping the stack sorted as you push) solves 'next greater element', 'daily temperatures' and 'largest rectangle in a histogram' in O(n). It is a high-yield follow-up.
'Solve this without recursion' means 'use an explicit stack'.

quiz.question:
push(1); push(2); push(3); pop(); push(4); pop(); pop();
What is the last value popped?
quiz.explanation: Stack after pushes 1,2,3 is [1,2,3]. pop→3, push 4 →[1,2,4], pop→4, pop→2. The last popped value is 2.

quiz.question: 'Given daily temperatures, for each day find how many days until a warmer day.' Which structure?
options: Monotonic stack of indices waiting for a warmer day
quiz.explanation: Each day waits for the next warmer one — the most recent unresolved days resolve first, which is LIFO. Keeping a stack of decreasing temperatures gives O(n) instead of O(n²).

quiz.question: Why is `ArrayDeque` preferred over `java.util.Stack` in modern Java?
options: Stack extends Vector, so it is synchronised and slower with no benefit here
quiz.explanation: Both are O(1) per operation, but Vector's synchronisation costs on every call and is pointless for a single-threaded algorithm. The Java docs themselves recommend ArrayDeque.
